docs.title: Quick Add & Natural Language Parser API
docs.text: You can open the Quick Add Transaction dialog from the + icon in the top-right action strip or via the Command Palette (Ctrl+K → Quick Add Transaction). It lets you either enter a transaction directly (POST /api/add) or paste free-form text, click Parse Text, review suggestions/confidence scores, and save into add_journal_path (POST /api/parser/create-transaction).

docs.title: Natural Language Input Patterns
docs.text: The parser recognizes dates (2026-05-10, 20 Apr, 10 May 2026, today, yesterday, last friday), prefix/suffix/word amounts ($15.50, 15 USD, twenty rupees), account/payment hints (using bmo cc, from checking), and payee markers (at no frills).

docs.title: POST /api/parser/parse
docs.text:
Parses free-form transaction text and returns structured suggestions with confidence scores.

Request body:

{
  "text": "20 Apr spent $15 at grocery store using credit card"
}

Response body:

{
  "result": {
    "date": "2026-04-20T00:00:00Z",
    "amount": "15",
    "currency": "USD",
    "payee": "grocery store",
    "from_account": "Liabilities:CreditCard:Visa",
    "to_account": "Expenses:Groceries",
    "direction": "expense",
    "confidence": {
      "date": 0.8,
      "amount": 0.95,
      "payee": 0.8,
      "from_account": 0.72,
      "to_account": 0.81,
      "direction": 0.85,
      "overall": 0.82
    },
    "suggestions": [],
    "warnings": []
  },
  "auto_create": false,
  "requires_confirmation": true
}

docs.title: POST /api/parser/create-transaction
docs.text:
Parses free-form text, applies optional user overrides (including narration and multi-currency conversion fields), appends and validates the transaction in add_journal_path, and asynchronously logs training feedback. Note: this endpoint writes and validates the file on disk and does not trigger a sync automatically — trigger a journal sync afterward to refresh reports.

Request body:

{
  "text": "paid $20 for lunch using debit",
  "date": "2026-05-10",
  "payee": "Lunch",
  "narration": "Team lunch",
  "from_account": "Assets:Checking",
  "to_account": "Expenses:Dining",
  "amount": "20",
  "commodity": "USD",
  "to_amount": "1670",
  "to_commodity": "INR",
  "exchange_rate": "83.5",
  "suggestion_used": 1,
  "time_to_confirm_ms": 1200
}

narration, to_amount, to_commodity, and exchange_rate are optional.

Response body:

{
  "success": true,
  "entry": "2026/05/10 * Lunch\n  Assets:Checking  -20 USD\n  Expenses:Dining   20 USD\n",
  "errors": [],
  "final_transaction": {
    "date": "2026-05-10",
    "payee": "Lunch",
    "from_account": "Assets:Checking",
    "to_account": "Expenses:Dining",
    "amount": "20",
    "commodity": "USD"
  },
  "parser_confidence": {
    "overall": 0.82
  },
  "parser_suggestions": []
}

docs.title: Error Handling
docs.text:
Both endpoints use the standard error envelope:

{
  "error": {
    "code": "INVALID_REQUEST",
    "message": "..."
  }
}

Possible codes include: - INVALID_REQUEST for malformed JSON or invalid field values - INTERNAL_ERROR for unexpected server-side failures - READONLY when write endpoint is blocked by readonly mode - UNAUTHORIZED when auth fails

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• POST /api/parser/parse is a read operation and does not mutate data.
  • POST /api/parser/create-transaction is a write operation and is protected by readonly middleware.
  • On low-confidence parse results, clients should show account suggestions and allow user correction before create.

docs.title: Phase 0 Performance Baseline (config/dashboard/projection)
docs.text: This baseline captures endpoint latency and SQL workload before performance refactors.

docs.title: Reproducible run steps
docs.text:
From repo root:

go run ./cmd/perfbaseline --iterations 30 --warmup 5 --years 20

The harness:

  • creates a temporary SQLite database
  • seeds a synthetic 20-year monthly dataset
  • calls:
  • GET /api/config
  • GET /api/dashboard
  • GET /api/networth/projection
  • collects:
  • request latency (p50, p95)
  • SQL query count
  • total SQL time

Telemetry comes from response headers emitted by the handlers:

  • X-Paisa-Perf-Latency-Ms
  • X-Paisa-Perf-SQL-Count
  • X-Paisa-Perf-SQL-Time-Ms

docs.title: Baseline results (Phase 0)
docs.text:
Captured at 2026-05-16T13:14:42Z on:

  • Go go1.24.13
  • linux/amd64
  • 4 vCPUs

Dataset: synthetic 20 years (5 warmup + 30 measured samples per endpoint)

endpoint p50 latency (ms) p95 latency (ms) total sql queries total sql time (ms) avg sql queries/request avg sql time/request (ms) /api/config 1.24 2.10 60 3.94 2.00 0.13 /api/dashboard 106.77 120.31 570 2432.93 19.00 81.10 /api/networth/projection 32.71 35.73 120 406.03 4.00 13.53

docs.title: Before/after comparison template
docs.text:
Use this checklist for each optimization phase:

  • Run the same harness command (cmd/perfbaseline) with same flags.
  • Record machine/runtime context (OS, arch, CPU count, Go version).
  • Compare p50/p95 for all 3 endpoints.
  • Compare total SQL query count per endpoint.
  • Compare total SQL time per endpoint.
  • Flag any regression (>10% p95 increase) with root-cause notes.
  • Link PR/commit implementing the phase optimization.

docs.title: Phase 5 Query Plan Tuning (long-history journals)
docs.text: This phase targets SQLite posting scans that dominate dashboard/projection input derivation on 20+ year ledgers.

docs.title: Added indexes
docs.text:
Migration v12 adds:

  • idx_postings_forecast_date on (forecast, date)
  • idx_postings_forecast_account_date on (forecast, account, date)

Both indexes are created with CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS, so migration is safe for fresh installs and existing databases.

docs.title: Query-plan verification
docs.text:
Use SQLite EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN for representative predicates:

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM postings
WHERE forecast = 0 AND account LIKE 'Income:%' AND date >= ? AND date < ?
ORDER BY date ASC, amount DESC, account ASC;

EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN
SELECT * FROM postings
WHERE forecast = 0 AND date < ?
ORDER BY date ASC, amount DESC, account ASC;

Expected plan output includes:

  • idx_postings_forecast_account_date for account-prefix + date-range scans
  • idx_postings_forecast_date for forecast + date-range scans

Automated coverage exists in internal/model/migration/migration_test.go (TestV12Migration_ExplainUsesPostingReadIndexes).

docs.title: Rollout
docs.text:
1. Deploy binary containing migration v12.
  2. On startup, migration.RunMigrations applies v12 and records schema version 12.
  3. Validate via:
  4. SELECT version FROM schema_versions ORDER BY version DESC LIMIT 1;
  5. SELECT name FROM sqlite_master WHERE type='index' AND name LIKE 'idx_postings_forecast%';

docs.title: Rollback
docs.text:
If rollback is required:

  1. DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_postings_forecast_account_date;
  2. DROP INDEX IF EXISTS idx_postings_forecast_date;
  3. Optionally keep schema_versions at 12 and run older binaries in read-only mode, or ship a follow-up migration if strict downgrade support is required.

No table shape or data payload changes are introduced in v12; rollback only removes secondary indexes.

docs.title: Financial Planning & Life Projections
docs.text:
Paisa features a Planning suite that turns your historical double-entry accounting records into deterministic projections, stochastic Monte Carlo life simulations, life-goal tracking, scenario stress-testing, and tax-aware drawdown strategies.

In the default Grouped navigation layout, Planning contains Projections & Life Plan, Financial Goals, and (when default_currency is INR) Tax.

The planning modules include:

  1. Life Plan & Financial DNA (/planning/life) — Personal financial profiling, goal markers, and Monte Carlo net worth simulation.
  2. Net Worth Projections (/planning/projection) — Multi-scenario deterministic curves (Conservative, Expected, Optimistic) with precision inputs, Financial DNA calibration, year-by-year breakdown tables, and CSV export.
  3. What-If Scenarios (/planning/life/whatif) — Comparative Monte Carlo stress testing against your baseline plan.
  4. Tax-Aware Drawdown Strategy (/planning/life/drawdown) — Priority-bucketed withdrawal ordering and capital-gains tax optimization over FIFO lots.
  5. Milestone Life Goals (/planning/life/goals) — One-off milestone and recurring goals integrated directly into life simulations.
  6. Retirement & Savings Goals (/planning/goals) — Config-backed target trackers (see Goals).

docs.title: 1. Financial DNA Extraction & Monte Carlo Simulation
docs.text:
Navigating to Planning → Life Plan & DNA (/planning/life; Classic: Planning → Life Plan) extracts your Financial DNA (GET /api/projection/dna) from historical ledger data:

  • Annual Income & Income Growth Rate: Derived from historical Income:* postings.
  • Annual Expenses & Expense Growth Rate: Trailing living costs (excluding Expenses:Tax).
  • Savings Rate & Monthly Contribution: Derived from actual historical net investments vs. net income.
  • Historical Return & Volatility ($\sigma$): Calculated across your portfolio price history.

docs.title: Interactive Simulation Parameters
docs.text:
Adjust slider controls to run stochastic simulations (POST /api/projection/simulate):

  • Projection Years: 5 to 50 years (default 30).
  • Expected Return (%): 0 to 30%.
  • Volatility (Risk %): 0 to 40%.
  • Monthly Contribution: Ongoing monthly savings additions.
  • Contribution Growth (%): 0 to 20% annual increment rate.
  • Inflation Rate (%): 0 to 15%.
  • Safe Withdrawal Rate (SWR %): 2 to 8%.
  • Iterations: 100 to 10,000 stochastic Monte Carlo paths (step 100, default 1,000).

Simulation results are cached in memory by normalized configuration and automatically invalidated whenever a journal or price sync completes.

docs.title: Monte Carlo Fan Chart, Goals & FIRE Timeline
docs.text: The chart plots percentile bands (P10, P25, P50 (Median), P75, and P90) alongside configured Milestone Life Goals as timeline markers and probability cards showing each goal's funding likelihood.

docs.title: 2. Deterministic Net Worth Projections
docs.text:
Under Planning → Projections & Life Plan → Net Worth Projections (/planning/projection), Paisa computes Conservative (6% default), Expected (9% default), and Optimistic (12% default) trajectories alongside Current Net Worth, Monthly Contribution, Annual Expenses, Target Corpus, Years to FIRE, and FIRE Progress:

  • Every parameter includes both a slider and a precision numeric input box for exact values or horizons beyond the slider range.
  • Your Financial DNA displays extracted income/expense growth, savings rate, and historical return/volatility, with an Apply to Sliders button to calibrate the projection from your ledger history.
  • Year-by-Year Projection Tables list Year, Starting Corpus, Annual Contribution, Return, Ending Corpus, and Inflated Expenses for all three scenarios, with an Export CSV button for each scenario.

See Assets – Projection (FIRE) for the exact formulas.

docs.title: 3. Milestone & Recurring Life Goals
docs.text:
Under Planning → Financial Goals → Milestone Life Goals (/planning/life/goals), you can create and prioritize life goals stored under goals.life[] in paisa.yaml:

  • Goal Types (two supported types):
  • milestone: One-time lump-sum outflow requiring Target Amount and Target Month (YYYY-MM).
  • recurring: Repeated outflow requiring Start Month (YYYY-MM), End Month (YYYY-MM), Frequency (monthly, quarterly, or yearly), and Allocation Per Occurrence (monthly_allocation).
  • Additional Parameters: Name, Icon, Inflation Override (%) (optional per-goal override), Priority (assigned from list order; higher-priority goals are funded first), and Funded By accounts.
goals:
  life:
    - name: House Down Payment
      icon: mdi:home
      type: milestone
      target_amount: 2000000
      target_date: "2029-06"
      priority: 2
      funded_by:
        - Assets:Debt:*
    - name: College Tuition
      icon: mdi:school
      type: recurring
      start_date: "2032-06"
      end_date: "2036-05"
      frequency: yearly
      inflation_rate: 8
      priority: 1
      monthly_allocation: 400000
      funded_by:
        - Assets:Equity:*

docs.title: 4. What-If Scenario Stress Testing
docs.text:
The What-If Scenarios workspace (/planning/life/whatif, backed by POST /api/projection/whatif) runs your baseline plan side-by-side against up to five alternate scenarios using the same goal-aware Monte Carlo engine.

  • Prebuilt Templates: Increase SIP by 10k, Job loss for 6 months, and Early retirement, plus Add Custom Scenario.
  • Summary Cards & Overlay Chart: Displays Baseline FIRE (%), Target Corpus, Median FIRE Year (fire_year_p50), and Active Goals, alongside interactive scenario toggles overlaid on the Baseline P25–P75 fan band and a comparison table.

docs.title: 5. Tax-Aware Drawdown Strategy
docs.text:
The Tax-Aware Drawdown module (/planning/life/drawdown, backed by POST /api/projection/drawdown) ranks which asset lots to liquidate first to meet a target withdrawal amount while minimizing estimated capital gains tax.

Only asset accounts holding commodities configured with a supported tax_category (equity, equity65, equity35, debt, unlisted_equity) appear in the eligible assets pool.

docs.title: Priority Buckets, Drag-and-Drop & Auto-Grouping
docs.text:
• Strategy Buckets: Order priority buckets (Priority 1, Priority 2, …). Each bucket supports:
  • Explicit Assigned Assets: Drag asset chips from Unassigned Assets directly into buckets (or click Clear to revert to rule matching).
  • Account Glob: Pattern filter such as Assets:Equity:* (used when explicit accounts are not set on the bucket).
  • Match Tax Category: Filter lots matching a specific commodity tax category.
  • Apply Tax As (override_tax_category): Override how matched lots in this bucket are taxed during drawdown analysis without changing global paisa.yaml commodity definitions.
  • Min Holding Period (Months): Require lots to meet a minimum age before becoming eligible for the bucket.
  • One-Click Auto-Group: Seed buckets automatically with live bucket-count previews via Auto-group: Account Family, Auto-group: Tax Category, or Auto-group: Current Rules.

docs.title: Lot Selection & Projection Impact
docs.text:
For a target withdrawal amount:

  1. Paisa inspects open FIFO lots across eligible asset accounts and evaluates buckets in priority order.
  2. Within each bucket, eligible lots are sorted by lowest effective tax rate, then lowest total tax amount, then longest holding duration.
  3. Withdrawals cascade from higher-priority buckets into subsequent buckets until the requested amount is covered (reporting any uncovered shortfall if insufficient eligible lots exist).
  4. The UI shows covered vs. uncovered amounts, total estimated tax, post-tax net proceeds, optional Monte Carlo Projection Impact, and per-lot sale recommendations (units, purchase date, holding days, tax breakdown, and effective rate).

docs.title: Related Guides
docs.text:
• Goals (Retirement & Savings)
  • Tax Harvesting, Capital Gains & Schedule AL (INR journals)

docs.title: Recurring
docs.text:
Open Cash Flow → Flows & Recurring → Recurring Bills (Classic: Cash Flow → Recurring, /cash_flow/recurring) to track expected bills, EMIs, and periodic income or investments.

Some of the transactions recur on a regular interval and it might be useful to know the next due date for such transactions. The Recurring page shows upcoming, cleared, and recently missed transactions alongside a navbar status legend (Cleared, Cleared late, Past due, and Upcoming). You can also monitor recurring schedules directly from the Recurring widget on your Dashboard (configurable 1–30 items, default 16).

Paisa depends on the posting metadata to identify which transactions are recurring. This metadata can be added in couple of ways. Let's say you pay rent every month and you want to mark it as recurring, a typical journal would like below

2023/07/01 Rent
    Expenses:Rent             15,000 INR
    Assets:Checking

2023/08/01 Rent
    Expenses:Rent             15,000 INR
    Assets:Checking

You can manually tag a posting by adding ; Recurring: Rent.

2023/07/01 Rent
    ; Recurring: Rent
    Expenses:Rent             15,000 INR
    Assets:Checking

2023/08/01 Rent
    ; Recurring: Rent
    Expenses:Rent             15,000 INR
    Assets:Checking

The first part of the metadata before the colon is called tag name. It should be Recurring. The second part is the tag value. This value is used to group transactions.

Tagging each and every posting can be tiresome. Ledger has a feature called Automated Transaction which can make this process simpler.

= Expenses:Rent
    ; Recurring: Rent

The first line is the predicate and the line below it will get added to any matching posting. By default, it will match the posting account name. But you can target other attributes like payee, amount etc. You can find more examples below, more info about predicate is available on Ledger docs

= expr payee=~/^PPF$/
    ; Recurring: PPF

= expr payee=~/Mutual Fund/
    ; Recurring: Mutual Fund

= expr 'account=~/Expenses:Insurance/ and (payee=~/HDFC/)'
    ; Recurring: Life Insurance

= expr 'account=~/Expenses:Insurance/ and !(payee=~/HDFC/)'
    ; Recurring: Bike Insurance

= expr payee=~/Savings Interest/
    ; Recurring: Savings Interest

Tip

Include the automated transactions at the top of the main ledger file. Ledger will apply the rules only to transactions that follow the automated transactions.

docs.title: Period
docs.text:
Paisa will try to infer the recurring period of the transactions automatically, but this might not be perfect. Recurring period can also be explicitly specified via metadata.

= expr payee=~/Savings Interest/
    ; Recurring: Savings Interest
    ; Period: L MAR,JUN,SEP,DEC ?

Let's say your bank deposits the interest on the last day of the last month of the quarter, we can specify like the example above. Paisa editor recognizes period syntax and shows the upcoming 3 schedules right next to period metadata.

┌─────────── day of the month 1-31
│  ┌─────────── month 1-12 or JAN-DEC
│  │  ┌─────────── day of the week 0-6 (Sunday to Saturday)
│  │  │
1  *  ?

The syntax of the period is similar to cron, with the omission of seconds and hours.

Field Allowed values Special characters Day of month 1–31 * , - ? L W Month 1-12 or JAN-DEC * , - Day of week 0-6 or SUN-SAT * , - ? L

* also known as wildcard represents all valid values. ? means you want to omit the field, usually you use it on the day of month or day of week. L means last day of the month or week. , can be used to specify multiple entries. - can be used to specify range. W means the closest business day to given day of month

Multiple cron expressions can be specified by joining them using |. Refer the wikipedia for more information. If you are not sure, just type it out and the editor will show you whether it is valid and the next 3 schedules if valid.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Last day of every month ; Period: L * ?
  • 5th every month ; Period: 5 * ?
  • Every Sunday ; Period: ? * 0
  • 1st of Jan and 7th of Feb ; Period: 1 JAN ? | 7 FEB ?
  • Closest business day to the 15th day of every month. ; Period: 15W * ?

Warning

Recurring page will only display a transaction as recurring if there is more than one transaction with the same tag name. If you have only one transaction, wait until the next transaction is added to see it on the recurring page.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Paisa now maintains a single consolidated roadmap in ../roadmap.md.

Use that document as the source of truth for strategy, quarter-by-quarter delivery, technical enablers, and guardrails.

docs.title: Sheets
docs.text: Open Tools → Sheets (Classic: More → Sheets, /more/sheets) to launch Paisa's interactive financial notepad calculator. Sheet files are stored in sheets_directory (configurable under Tools → Configuration → General → Core Setup) and are automatically included in .zip archives created via Backup & Export.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Sheet is a notepad calculator that computes the answer as you type. It has full access to your ledger and can be used to calculate the answers for a wide variety of financial questions.

Experimental

Sheet is an experimental feature. Give it a try and let me know how it goes, specially what is missing and what can be improved. The syntax and semantics of sheet may change in future releases.

docs.title: Calculator
docs.text:
Sheet can act as a normal calculator. The example below shows how to calculate the monthly EMI for a home loan.

# Home Loan
price = 40,00,000
down_payment = 20% * price
finance_amount = price - down_payment
interest_rate = 8.6%
term = 30

n = term * 12
r = interest_rate / 12
# EMI
monthly_payment = r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (-n)) * finance_amount

# Home Loan
40,00,000
8,00,000
32,00,000
0
30

360
0
# EMI
24832

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
Sheets comes with a set of built-in functions. You can also define your own functions. The example below shows how to define a function

# Years to Double
years_to_double(rate) = 72 / rate

years_to_double(2)
years_to_double(4)
years_to_double(6)
years_to_double(8)
years_to_double(10)
years_to_double(12)
years_to_double(14)

# Years to Double


36
18
12
9
7
6
5

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
Query is what makes sheets powerful. It allows you to query your ledger postings and do calculations on them. The example below shows how to calculate cost basis of your assets so you can report them to Income Tax department.

# Schedule AL
date_query = {date <= [2023-03-31]}
cost_basis(x) = cost(fifo(x AND date_query))
cost_basis_negative(x) = cost(fifo(negate(x AND date_query)))

# Immovable
immovable = cost_basis({account = Assets:House})

# Movable
metal = 0
art = 0
vehicle = 0
bank = cost_basis({account =~ /^Assets:Checking/})
share = cost_basis({account =~ /^Assets:Equity:.*/ OR
                    account =~ /^Assets:Debt:.*/})
insurance = 0
loan = 0
cash = 0

# Liability
liability = cost_basis_negative({account =~ /^Liabilities:Homeloan/})

# Total
total = immovable + metal + art + vehicle + bank + share + insurance + loan + cash - liability

# Schedule AL




# Immovable
25,00,000

# Movable
0
0
0
1,21,402
66,98,880

0
0
0

# Liability
6,21,600

# Total
86,98,682

docs.title: Number
docs.text:
Sheet allows comma as a separator. % is a syntax sugar for dividing the number by 100. So 8% is same as 0.08.

100,00
100.00
-100
8%

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Sheet supports the following operators. ^ is the exponentiation operator.

1 + 1
1 - 1
1 * 1
1 / 1
1 ^ 2

docs.title: Variable
docs.text:
You can define variables using = operator. Variables have to be defined before they are used.

x = 1
y = 2

z = x + y

docs.title: Function
docs.text:
Sheet comes with a set of built-in functions. You can also define your own functions. Function definition starts with the function name and then a list of arguments. The body of the function is a single expression. To call a function, use the function name followed by arguments.

sum(a, b) = a + b

sum(1, 2)

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
Query is a first class citizen in sheet. You can think of a query as a list of postings that match the conditions. The query syntax is same as the search syntax used in postings and transactions pages. It has to be enclosed inside a {}. Query can be treated as any other value, can be passed as an argument, can be assigned to a variable. In fact you can combine two queries using AND and OR operator as well.

query = {account = Expenses:Utilities AND payee =~ /uber/i}

upto_this_fy = {date < [2024-04-01]}
assets = { account =~ /^Assets:.*/ }
liabilities = { account =~ /^Liabilities:.*/ }

assets_upto_this_fy = upto_this_fy AND assets
liabilities_upto_this_fy = upto_this_fy AND liabilities
What is posting? 

2022/01/01 Salary
    Income:Salary:Acme        -100,000 INR
    Assets:Checking            100,000 INR
In the above transaction, there are two postings. A transaction consists of several postings that sum to zero. If you want to know the cost of your checking account, you would use cost({account = Assets:Checking})

docs.title: Comment
docs.text:
Sheet supports single line comments starting with ; or //.

// set x
x = 1
; set y
y = 2

z = x + y // add x and y

docs.title: Functions
docs.text: You can find the full list of built-in functions here. This list is very slim as of now, please start a discussion if you want some functions to be added here.

docs.title: cost(q: Posting[] | Query): number
docs.text: Returns the sum of the cost of all the postings.

docs.title: balance(q: Posting[] | Query): number
docs.text: Returns the sum of the current market value of all the postings.

docs.title: fifo(q: Posting[] | Query): Posting[]
docs.text:
Returns the list of postings after performing a FIFO adjustment. For example, assume you have 3 postings

2020/01/01 Buy
    Assets:Bank:Checking   100 USD
2020/02/01 Buy
    Assets:Bank:Checking   100 USD
2020/03/01 Sell
    Assets:Bank:Checking   -50 USD

after FIFO adjustment, you will get the following postings

2020/01/01 Buy
    Assets:Bank:Checking    50 USD
2020/02/01 Buy
    Assets:Bank:Checking   100 USD

All your sell postings will be adjusted against the oldest buy postings and you will have the remaining buy postings.

docs.title: negate(q: Posting[] | Query): Posting[]
docs.text: Negates the amount and quantity of all the postings. This would be useful when you want to do some calculation on liabilities or income which are negative in nature.

docs.title: Use Cases & Sample Queries
docs.text: Because Sheets combines a live calculator with direct queries against your ledger, you can build dynamic financial worksheets that update automatically as you add new transactions. Below are common use cases and sample queries you can adapt to your own account hierarchy.

docs.title: 1. Net Worth & Unrealized Gains
docs.text:
Compare the FIFO cost basis of your assets against their current market value, subtract liabilities, and calculate total unrealized gains.

# Net Worth & Unrealized Gains
assets = {account =~ /^Assets:/}
liabilities = {account =~ /^Liabilities:/}
investments = {account =~ /^Assets:(Equity|Debt|MutualFunds):/}

// Current market value vs. FIFO cost basis
total_assets = balance(assets)
total_liabilities = balance(negate(liabilities))
net_worth = total_assets - total_liabilities

// Investment performance
invested_cost = cost(fifo(investments))
invested_value = balance(investments)
unrealized_gain = invested_value - invested_cost
return_pct = (unrealized_gain / invested_cost) * 100

docs.title: 2. Savings Rate & Cash Flow
docs.text:
Track how much of your income you are saving over a given period (such as a financial year or [this year], [last month]). Since income postings are negative in double-entry accounting, wrap them with negate(...).

# Annual Savings Rate
period = {date >= [2025-04-01] AND date <= [2026-03-31]}

income = cost(negate({account =~ /^Income:/} AND period))
expenses = cost({account =~ /^Expenses:/} AND period)

net_savings = income - expenses
savings_rate_pct = (net_savings / income) * 100
monthly_avg_expense = expenses / 12

docs.title: 3. Emergency Fund Runway & FIRE Progress
docs.text:
Use your actual historical spending from the ledger to size your emergency fund and track progress toward Financial Independence (FIRE).

# Emergency Fund & FIRE
annual_expenses = cost({account =~ /^Expenses:/ AND date >= [last year]})
monthly_expenses = annual_expenses / 12

// Liquid cash available in checking/savings accounts
liquid_cash = balance({account =~ /^Assets:(Checking|Savings)/})
runway_months = liquid_cash / monthly_expenses

// FIRE target using the 4% safe withdrawal rate (25x annual expenses)
swr = 4%
fire_target = annual_expenses / swr
portfolio = balance({account =~ /^Assets:(Equity|Debt|MutualFunds):/})
fire_progress_pct = (portfolio / fire_target) * 100

docs.title: 4. Portfolio Rebalancing Calculator
docs.text:
Check your current asset allocation and calculate the exact amount to buy or sell to return to your target split.

# Portfolio Rebalancing
equity = balance({account =~ /^Assets:Equity:/})
debt = balance({account =~ /^Assets:Debt:/})
total_portfolio = equity + debt

// Current allocation (%)
equity_pct = (equity / total_portfolio) * 100
debt_pct = (debt / total_portfolio) * 100

// Target 70% Equity / 30% Debt
target_equity = total_portfolio * 70%
target_debt = total_portfolio * 30%

// Positive = buy, Negative = sell
equity_rebalance = target_equity - equity
debt_rebalance = target_debt - debt

docs.title: 5. Spending by Category, Merchant, or Tag
docs.text:
Combine account, payee, note, and date filters to inspect specific spending habits or gather figures for tax deductions and reimbursements.

# Category & Merchant Insights
fy = {date >= [2025-04-01] AND date <= [2026-03-31]}

// Food delivery spend across multiple merchants
food_delivery = cost({payee =~ /swiggy|zomato/i} AND fy)

// Reimbursable or tax-deductible expenses tagged in transaction notes
tax_deductible = cost({account =~ /^Expenses:/ AND note =~ /tax-deductible/i} AND fy)
reimbursable = cost({note =~ /reimbursable/i} AND fy)

// Large discretionary purchases over 5,000
large_expenses = cost({account =~ /^Expenses:/ AND total > 5000} AND fy)

docs.title: 6. Loan Principal & Interest Tracking
docs.text:
Monitor remaining loan principal alongside total interest paid to date, and compare against a target payoff payment.

# Home Loan Tracker
loan_principal = cost(fifo(negate({account =~ /^Liabilities:Homeloan/})))
interest_paid = cost({account = Expenses:Interest:Homeloan})
interest_this_fy = cost({account = Expenses:Interest:Homeloan AND date >= [2025-04-01]})

// Simulate monthly EMI for the remaining balance
annual_rate = 8.5%
remaining_months = 180
r = annual_rate / 12
estimated_emi = r / (1 - (1 + r) ^ (-remaining_months)) * loan_principal

docs.title: Data Synchronization
docs.text: Paisa keeps its SQLite read model synchronized with your plain-text journal files and external market price providers.

docs.title: Manual & Background Sync
docs.text:
Trigger synchronization anytime from the top-right action bar:

  • Sync Journal: Re-parses your journal files and updates postings and snapshots.
  • Update Prices: Fetches latest quotes from configured price providers. Use Force Refresh on Ledger → Commodity Prices (/ledger/price) to pass force_prices: true and rebuild full price history.
  • Update Mutual Fund Portfolios: Updates underlying fund portfolio compositions.

docs.title: Async Sync & Job Tracking
docs.text: POST /api/sync returns 202 Accepted immediately with a job ID ({ "job_id": "<uuid>" }). Work runs asynchronously in a SQLite-backed queue so in-flight jobs survive process restarts, while the UI subscribes to Server-Sent Events (GET /api/jobs/stream) for live progress updates.

docs.title: Lazy Snapshot Refresh
docs.text: To minimize wall-clock sync latency, Paisa marks cached read-model snapshots (dashboard, projection, investment_income) dirty when journal or price data changes and lazily rebuilds each snapshot on first access (or prioritizes the active view via active_snapshot).

docs.title: Incremental Price Sync Optimization
docs.text:
Price providers use incremental fetching to keep updates fast:

  • Yahoo Finance (com-yahoo) passes incremental period1 timestamps since the last cached price date.
  • Alpha Vantage (co-alphavantage) switches to outputsize=compact when incremental history is within 80 days.
  • Database writes use batched SQLite upserts.

docs.title: Sync History Overlay
docs.text:
Click the clock-rotate-left icon in the top-right action bar to open Sync History. It displays jobs in reverse-chronological order with status badges, timestamps, live-ticking wall-clock durations for active jobs, commodity progress counts, error snippets, and expandable step details.

Clicking Clear history calls POST /api/jobs/clear to remove terminal (completed/failed) jobs from both the server queue and the UI.

docs.title: Automatic Freshness & External File Change Detection
docs.text:
The top-right action bar shows live freshness indicators:

  • Update Prices icon: Turns amber when the last price sync is $\ge 24$ hours old and red when it is $\ge 48$ hours old (or never run).
  • Sync Journal icon: Turns amber whenever journal files change on disk. Paisa runs a background JournalWatcher (comparing file modification times and SHA-256 hashes across your main journal and all included files) while the UI polls GET /api/journal/status every 30 seconds and on tab focus (visibilitychange), surfacing external edits made in your editor or via Git without needing a manual check.

docs.title: Scheduled Sync via CLI
docs.text:
Schedule automated syncs outside the web UI using paisa update:

# Sync journal, commodities, portfolios, and CII index
paisa update

# Sync individual targets
paisa update --journal      # -j
paisa update --commodity    # -c
paisa update --portfolio    # -p

docs.title: Automation Examples
docs.text:
• Windows: Use Task Scheduler to run paisa.exe update --commodity daily.
  • Linux / macOS: Add a cron job (crontab -e): 0 18 * * * /path/to/paisa update --commodity.
  • Docker: Execute from host cron: docker exec <container_name> paisa update -c.

docs.title: Firefly III Webhook Integration
docs.text: Paisa can receive transaction webhooks from Firefly III and automatically append new entries to add_journal_path.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. In paisa.yaml, set add_journal_path (Paisa creates parent directories and the file automatically if missing; make sure your main journal includes it):

    add_journal_path: /home/john/Documents/paisa/added.ledger

  2. In Firefly III, create a webhook pointing at http://<paisa-host>:7500/api/webhooks/firefly with the After transaction creation trigger (STORE_TRANSACTION events are processed; other webhook event types are ignored).

  3. Run Sync Journal (or scheduled paisa update --journal) to ingest the appended entries.

docs.title: Firefly III Reconciliation (Labs)
docs.text:
Labs Feature

Hidden by default. Enable labs.firefly_reconcile: true in paisa.yaml (or under Tools → Configuration → Tools → Labs).

When enabled, Tools → Reconciliation (/more/reconciliation; Classic: More → Reconciliation) compares your Paisa account balances against Firefly III and highlights discrepancies.

firefly:
  url: https://firefly.example.com
  token: your-personal-access-token
  ignore_accounts:
    - Assets:Cash

labs:
  firefly_reconcile: true

docs.title: User Authentication
docs.text:
You can setup username and password accounts to restrict access to the application. Open Tools → Configuration → General → Security & Auth (/more/config/security), expand User Accounts, and click the icon to add a new username and password. Once you save the configuration, you will be logged out if you had not already signed in with an account.

Authentication guards all protected API routes under /api/* and Connect-RPC endpoints under /connect/* (except /api/ping, /api/auth/login, and /api/auth/logout). If someone has shell or filesystem access to the host directory containing your journal files, paisa.yaml, or paisa.db, they can still read those files directly.

HTTPS is required for internet-facing deployments

If you run Paisa on a server and access it over the public internet, you must use it over HTTPS and choose a strong password. Over plain HTTP, a man-in-the-middle attacker can capture your session token and gain full access to your financial data. See the Deployment guide for reverse-proxy TLS setup instructions.

docs.title: Session model
docs.text:
When you log in, Paisa creates a short-lived session and returns a session token (a random UUID). This token is stored in the browser and sent with every subsequent request in the X-Auth header.

Property Value Token format UUID v4 (random, 128-bit) Token lifetime 24 hours from login Storage SQLite sessions table on the server Revocation Logging out deletes the token immediately

Session tokens expire automatically after 24 hours. Logging out (POST /api/auth/logout) revokes the token immediately, regardless of the remaining lifetime.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Invalid token / failed auth probing Failed authentication attempts on protected /api/* and /connect/* endpoints are throttled by TokenAuthMiddleware (6 requests per minute, burst 3). Note that POST /api/auth/login itself is not rate-limited by Paisa — configure rate limiting at your reverse proxy for internet-facing deployments. Token theft over the network Tokens must only ever be transmitted over HTTPS (see warning above) Token theft from config file Tokens are not stored in paisa.yaml; only password hashes are Exposure via backup archives .zip downloads from Tools → Configuration → Tools → Backup & Export replace user_accounts passwords with [REDACTED] by default unless you explicitly opt in to include secrets Session fixation / forgery Tokens are cryptographically random UUIDs issued only after a successful login Persistent access after logout Logout deletes the token from the database immediately Offline password cracking (stolen config file) Passwords are hashed with SHA-256. While this prevents casual inspection, a determined attacker with access to paisa.yaml could attempt offline brute-force. Use a long, randomly-generated password and restrict file-system access to paisa.yaml to limit this risk.

docs.title: Password storage
docs.text:
Paisa uses the SHA-256 cryptographic hash function to convert your password into a digest before storing it in the configuration file. This means:

  • No one can read the configuration file and recover the password.
  • If you forget the password you can remove the user accounts from the configuration file to regain access.

Passwords are stored in paisa.yaml in the form sha256:<hex-digest>.

Use a strong, randomly-generated password

Paisa currently uses SHA-256 to hash passwords, which is a fast hash. If an attacker obtains a copy of paisa.yaml, they may be able to recover a weak password offline very quickly. Always use a long, randomly-generated password (16+ characters) and restrict read access to paisa.yaml on the server.

docs.title: Login flow
docs.text:
1. Browser sends POST /api/auth/login with {"username": "…", "password": "…"}.
  2. Server hashes the supplied password with SHA-256 and compares it to the stored hash using a constant-time comparison (preventing timing attacks).
  3. On success, a new session record is created in the database and the server returns {"token": "<uuid>", "expires_at": "…", "username": "…"}.
  4. The browser stores the token and includes it as X-Auth: <token> on all subsequent requests.
  5. Each request is validated against the sessions table; expired or non-existent tokens are rejected with HTTP 401.

docs.title: Legacy credential header
docs.text:
For backward compatibility, Paisa also supports a legacy authentication mode where credentials are sent directly in every request as X-Auth: username:plaintext-password. This mode is disabled by default and should not be used for internet-facing deployments. It can be enabled in paisa.yaml for automated scripts or API clients that cannot maintain sessions:

allow_legacy_auth: true

Disable this option once all clients have migrated to the session-based login flow.

docs.title: Goals
docs.text:
Goals help you track financial objectives and measure progress against your real ledger balances. Paisa supports three complementary goal systems:

  1. Retirement — Target corpus calculated from Safe Withdrawal Rate (SWR) and yearly expenses (/planning/goals).
  2. Savings — Fixed target amount with either a target date or planned periodic contribution (/planning/goals).
  3. Milestone & Recurring Life Goals — One-off milestones (milestone) and recurring cash outflows (recurring) modeled inside the Monte Carlo Life Plan (/planning/life/goals).

docs.title: Viewing & Managing Goals
docs.text:
• Retirement & Savings Goals: Open Planning → Financial Goals → Retirement & Savings Goals (/planning/goals; Classic: Planning → Goals) to inspect progress, drag to reorder priority, or click into each goal's detailed projection chart. Configure them in Tools → Configuration → Planning → Goals (/more/config/goals) or directly under goals: in paisa.yaml.
  • Milestone Life Goals: Open Planning → Financial Goals → Milestone Life Goals (/planning/life/goals) to add, edit, reorder, and save life goals directly in the UI.
  • Dashboard Widget: Configured retirement and savings goals can also be pinned to your Dashboard (configurable 1–12 items, ordered by descending priority).

docs.title: Retirement
docs.text:
Paisa helps you plan your retirement and track your progress on Planning → Financial Goals → Retirement & Savings Goals (/planning/goals). The first step is determining your target retirement corpus from your expected yearly expenses and Safe Withdrawal Rate (swr).

Both swr and savings (along with name and icon) are required fields when configuring a retirement goal under goals.retirement in Tools → Configuration → Planning → Goals (/more/config/goals) or in paisa.yaml.

goals:
  retirement:
    - name: Retirement
      icon: mdi:palm-tree
      swr: 3.3
      yearly_expenses: 1100000
      savings:
        - Assets:Equity:*
        - Assets:Debt:*

If you track expenses in Paisa, instead of hardcoding yearly_expenses, you can specify a list of expenses accounts. Paisa will compute the average of your last 3 years of expenses across those accounts:

goals:
  retirement:
    - name: Retirement
      icon: mdi:palm-tree
      swr: 2
      priority: 10
      expenses:
        - Expenses:Entertainment
        - Expenses:Gift
        - Expenses:Insurance
        - Expenses:Misc
        - Expenses:Shopping
        - Expenses:Utilities
      savings:
        - Assets:Equity:*
        - Assets:Debt:*

Set an optional integer priority to control display ordering — higher-priority goals appear first on the Dashboard Goals widget and /planning/goals.

docs.title: Savings
docs.text:
Savings represents a financial objective that you want to achieve, such as buying a car or house, funding a vacation, or building an emergency fund. View configured savings goals under Planning → Financial Goals → Retirement & Savings Goals (/planning/goals; Classic: Planning → Goals) and configure them in Tools → Configuration → Planning → Goals (/more/config/goals) or paisa.yaml.

goals:
  savings:
    - name: House
      target: 5000000
      icon: fluent-emoji-high-contrast:house-with-garden
      priority: 5
      accounts:
        - Assets:Equity:*
        - Assets:Debt:*

Specify the target amount and the accounts holding the earmarked funds. You can optionally set an integer priority (higher-priority goals are displayed first).

For modeling future outflows inside stochastic Monte Carlo projections, see Milestone & Recurring Life Goals.

docs.title: Forecast
docs.text:
When you save towards an objective, you will have a target date in mind. In the below config, you are specifying the target date and rate. Paisa will calculate the monthly contribution required to achieve the goal.

goals:
  savings:
    - name: House
      target: 5000000
      target_date: 2030-05-01
      rate: 10
      icon: fluent-emoji-high-contrast:house-with-garden
      accounts:
        - Assets:Equity:*
        - Assets:Debt:*

If on the other hand, you know how much you can afford to save every month, but want to know when the goal will be achieved, you can specify the payment per period and the rate. Paisa will calculate the target date.

goals:
  savings:
    - name: House
      target: 5000000
      payment_per_period: 50000
      rate: 10
      icon: fluent-emoji-high-contrast:house-with-garden
      accounts:
        - Assets:Equity:*
        - Assets:Debt:*

docs.title: Math
docs.text:
This section will give some rough idea of how the calculations are done. You can skip this section if you are not interested in the math.

F V + P V × ( 1 + R A T E ) N P E R + P M T × ( 1 + R A T E ) N P E R − 1 R A T E = 0 FV + PV \times (1+RATE)^{NPER} + PMT \times \frac{(1+RATE)^{NPER} - 1}{RATE} =0

Where

Variable Description Paisa FV Future Value target PV Present Value Current Savings PMT Payment per period payment_per_period / Monthly Investment needed RATE Rate of return rate NPER Number of periods target_date

Out of the 5 variables, if you know any 4, the 5th can be calculated by solving the equation. You can refer the blog post for more details.

docs.title: Tax
docs.text:
Paisa provides Indian tax-planning and reporting views under Planning → Tax in both Grouped and Classic navigation.

Currency visibility

The Tax navigation menu is displayed automatically when default_currency is set to INR in Configuration.

docs.title: Available Reports & Tools
docs.text:
• Tax Harvesting (/planning/tax/harvest) — Identify equity and debt lots eligible for long-term/short-term gain harvesting.
  • Capital Gains (/planning/tax/capital_gains) — Financial-year capital gains breakdown with FIFO lot matching, indexation/grandfathering rules, and slab vs. LTCG/STCG estimates.
  • Schedule AL (/planning/tax/schedule_al) — Asset and liability summary mapped to Indian Income Tax Schedule AL sections as of financial year-end.
  • Tax-Aware Drawdown Strategy (/planning/life/drawdown) — Order retirement withdrawals across priority buckets while estimating capital-gains tax impact.

docs.title: Disclaimer
docs.text: The author of this tool is not an accountant, the calculations are made based on their interpretation of rules and regulation. This tool is distributed free hoping it would be useful. The users are advised to consult a tax accountant before making any decision based on the information provided here. Check the LICENSE of paisa for more details.

docs.title: Capital Gains
docs.text:
Open Planning → Tax → Capital Gains (/planning/tax/capital_gains; shown when default_currency is INR) to review financial-year realized capital gains and estimated tax liability across mutual funds and stocks. The underlying lot-matching engine is also used by the Tax-Aware Drawdown Strategy planner.

Mutual Funds and equities are considered capital assets and capital gains tax applies on realized withdrawals. The Capital Gains page shows financial year wise capital gains tax based on your sell/redemption transactions, with the total summary, account-wise breakdown, and per buy/sell FIFO match details.

Only commodities with tax_category (equity, equity65, equity35, debt, or unlisted_equity) are included. Please check the Tax Harvesting page for configuration details.

docs.title: Gain
docs.text: The difference between the purchase and sell price.

docs.title: Taxable Gain
docs.text:
The gain after applying Indexation or Grandfathering provision.

Based on the duration between the purchase and sell date, an asset might be classified as Short Term or Long Term.

docs.title: Short Term Tax
docs.text: This would be a percentage of the Taxable Gain. The percentage varies based on the asset class.

docs.title: Long Term Tax
docs.text: This would be a percentage of the Taxable Gain. The percentage varies based on the asset class.

docs.title: Taxable at Slab Rate
docs.text: There are cases where the gain would be added to taxable income and charged Slab rate. Since the tax rate would depend on the person, the whole taxable amount is shown instead of the tax. You can multiply this with your slab rate to get the tax amount.

docs.title: Schedule AL
docs.text:
Open Planning → Tax → Schedule AL (/planning/tax/schedule_al; shown when default_currency is INR) to compute your end-of-year asset and liability totals by Schedule AL category. Use the financial year selector in the top navbar to switch between years.

As per Indian Income Tax rules, individuals with total income above ₹50 lakh are required to report Assets and Liabilities under Schedule AL. Paisa computes these totals using your configured account mappings.

code Section Details immovable A (1) Immovable Assets metal B (1) (i) Jewellery, bullion etc. art B (1) (ii) Archaeological collections, drawings, painting, sculpture or any work of art vehicle B (1) (iii) Vehicles, yachts, boats and aircrafts bank B (1) (iv) (a) Financial assets: Bank (including all deposits) share B (1) (iv) (b) Financial assets: Shares and securities insurance B (1) (iv) (c) Financial assets: Insurance policies loan B (1) (iv) (d) Financial assets: Loans and advances given cash B (1) (iv) (e) Financial assets: Cash in hand liability C (1) Liabilities

All you need to do is map your ledger accounts to each section under Tools → Configuration → Finance → Schedule AL (/more/config/schedule-al) or directly in paisa.yaml. Paisa computes the total as of the last day of the selected financial year.

schedule_al:
    - code: bank
      accounts:
          - Assets:Checking
    - code: share
      accounts:
          - Assets:Equity:*
          - Assets:Debt:*

docs.title: Tax Harvesting
docs.text:
Open Planning → Tax → Tax Harvesting (Classic: Planning → Tax → Harvest, /planning/tax/harvest; shown when default_currency is INR) to view holdings eligible for tax-loss or tax-gain harvesting.

Gains from asset types like Mutual Funds and Stocks are subject to capital gains tax. The taxation rate differs based on holding period, whether the asset is debt or equity, and annual exemption limits, and exit loads may also apply.

Paisa takes a flexible approach and lets you configure when each commodity is eligible to harvest under Tools → Configuration → Finance → Commodities & Prices (/more/config/commodities) or in paisa.yaml:

  1. harvest - specifies the number of holding days after which a lot is eligible for tax harvesting (for example, based on exit load and LTCG period).

  2. tax_category - defines how capital gains taxes are computed (applying applicable grandfathering, indexation, or slab rules):

    1. equity - Listed Indian equity shares and equity-oriented instruments.

    2. equity65 - Funds with 65% or more invested in Indian equity.

    3. equity35 - Funds with 35% or more (and less than 65%) invested in Indian equity.

    4. debt - Debt mutual funds and fixed-income instruments.

    5. unlisted_equity - Unlisted foreign or Indian equity.

commodities:
  - name: NIFTY
    type: mutualfund
    price:
      provider: in-mfapi
      code: 120716
    harvest: 365
    tax_category: equity65
  - name: ABCBF
    type: mutualfund
    price:
      provider: in-mfapi
      code: 119533
    harvest: 1095
    tax_category: debt

The tax harvest page will show the list of accounts eligible for harvesting.

docs.title: Multiple Folios
docs.text: Paisa uses FIFO method within an Account. If you have multiple folios, this might result in incorrect values. The issue can be solved by using a different Account for each folio.
